source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question A1

prompt: $a$ is the smallest positive integer greater than $1$ such that the sum of the first $a$ positive integers is a square. In other words, $a$ is the smallest positive integer such that $a>1$ and $1+2+3+\dots+a=b^2$, for some positive integer $b$. Find the value of $a+b$.

solutions.title: Triangular numbers
solutions.body:
The sums $1+2+\dots+a$ are $3,6,10,15,21,28,36,\dots$ for $a=2,3,4,\dots$. The first square is $36=6^2$, at $a=8$. So $a+b=8+6=14$.

**Answer: $14$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question A2

prompt: Let $T=14$. $p\diamond q$ is defined as $pq-(p+q)$. Evaluate $T\diamond7$. The answer is a two-digit number. Find its units digit.

solutions.title: Substitute
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from A1.) $14\diamond7=98-21=77$, whose units digit is $7$.

**Answer: $7$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question A3

prompt: Let $T=7$. A right-angled triangle has two sides $2T$ and $3T$. The longest side may be written as $a\sqrt b$, where $a$ and $b$ are primes. Find $a+b$.

solutions.title: Pythagoras
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from A2.) The two given sides are $14$ and $21$, and the longest side is the hypotenuse: $\sqrt{14^2+21^2}=7\sqrt{4+9}=7\sqrt{13}$. So $a=7$, $b=13$ and $a+b=20$.

**Answer: $20$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question A4

prompt: Let $T=20$. The line with equation $y=-x-1$ meets the parabola with equation $y=Tx^2-\frac12Tx$ at two points. The sum of the $x$-coordinates of these two points may be written as $\dfrac ab$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers with no common factor other than $1$. Find the value of $\dfrac ab$.

solutions.title: Sum of roots
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from A3.) Equating: $20x^2-10x=-x-1$, so $20x^2-9x+1=0$. This has two real roots (discriminant $81-80=1$), and their sum is $\frac9{20}$.

**Answer: $\frac9{20}$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question B1

prompt: The sum of three primes is $50$. Find the largest possible median of three such primes.

solutions.title: One prime must be 2
solutions.body:
The sum of three odd primes is odd, so one of the primes is $2$; the other two, $q\le r$, satisfy $q+r=48$ and the median is $q$. To make $q$ as large as possible with $q\le r$: $q=23$ would need $r=25$ (not prime), $q=24$ is not prime, and $q=19$, $r=29$ works. So the largest median is $19$.

**Answer: $19$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question B2

prompt: Let $T=19$. $x\diamond y$ is defined as $x^2-y$. The value of $\dfrac{T\diamond1}{T\diamond(-T)}$ is $\dfrac ab$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers with no common factor other than $1$. Find $a+b$.

solutions.title: Evaluate
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from B1.) $T\diamond1=361-1=360$ and $T\diamond(-T)=361+19=380$. The fraction is $\frac{360}{380}=\frac{18}{19}$, so $a+b=37$.

**Answer: $37$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question B3

prompt: Let $T=37$. $x=T^3$. Find the units digit of $x$.

solutions.title: Units digits
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from B2.) Only the units digit $7$ of $37$ matters: $7^3=343$, which ends in $3$.

**Answer: $3$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question B4

prompt: Let $T=3$. The point $A$ at $(T,4)$ is reflected in the $x$-axis to give point $B$. The point $B$ is reflected in the line $y=x$ to give point $C$. Find the area of the triangle $ABC$.

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from B3.) $A=(3,4)$, $B=(3,-4)$, $C=(-4,3)$. The side $AB$ is vertical with length $8$ and lies on the line $x=3$; the distance from $C$ to this line is $3-(-4)=7$. The area is $\frac12\cdot8\cdot7=28$.

**Answer: $28$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question C1

prompt: The table below shows an incomplete $4\times4$ magic square. Find the sum of the missing numbers divided by $6$. (In a magic square the sums of the numbers in each row, each column, and the two main diagonals are all the same.)

solutions.title: Use the complete row
solutions.body:
The bottom row gives the magic sum: $16+2+3+13=34$. Top row: $4+14+15+x=34$, so the top-right entry is $1$. First column: $4+9+c+16=34$, so the entry in the third row, first column is $5$. Third row: $5+d+10+8=34$ gives $d=11$. Second column: $14+a+11+2=34$ gives $a=7$. Second row: $9+7+b+12=34$ gives $b=6$. The missing numbers are $1,7,6,5,11$ with sum $30$, and $30/6=5$.

**Answer: $5$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question C2

prompt: Let $T=5$. A set of seven positive integers has mode $T$, median $2T-1$ and mean $3T-2$. Find the maximum possible value of the range of the seven integers.

solutions.title: Set up
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from C1.) The mode is $5$, the median is $9$ and the mean is $13$, so the sum is $91$. Write the integers in order $x_1\le\dots\le x_7$ with $x_4=9$. The range is $x_7-x_1=91-(2x_1+x_2+\dots+x_6)$, so we want $2x_1+x_2+\dots+x_6$ as small as possible.

The mode $5$ must occur more often than any other value, so at least twice, and $5\le9$ means two fives lie among $x_1,x_2,x_3$. The best choice is $x_1=1$, $x_2=x_3=5$ (if $x_1=5$ the range is smaller). The values above the median must not repeat any value as often as $5$ occurs (twice), and $9$ already occurs once at $x_4$; so $x_5\ge10$ and $x_6\ge11$ would be the smallest choices ($x_5=9$ would make $9$ appear twice, tying the mode; $x_5=x_6$ would also give a tie).

So $2x_1+x_2+\dots+x_6\ge2+5+5+9+10+11=42$ and the range is at most $91-42=49$. This is achieved by $1,5,5,9,10,11,50$ (mean $13$, median $9$, mode $5$).

**Answer: $49$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question C3

prompt: Let $T=49$. In the diagram, the points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on a circle. $BCE$ is a straight line. $AF$ is a tangent to the circle and $AF$ is parallel to $BD$. $\angle FAD=T^\circ$. $\angle DCE=x^\circ$. Find the sum of the digits of $x$.

solutions.title: Alternate segment theorem
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from C2.) Since $AF\parallel BD$, $\angle ADB=\angle FAD=49^\circ$ (alternate angles). By the alternate segment theorem, $\angle ABD=\angle FAD=49^\circ$. Triangle $ABD$ has angles $49^\circ,49^\circ$, so $\angle BAD=180-98=82^\circ$. The exterior angle of the cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ at $C$ equals the opposite interior angle: $\angle DCE=\angle BAD=82^\circ$. The digit sum of $82$ is $10$.

**Answer: $10$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question C4

prompt: Let $T=10$. Find the value of $\sqrt{\dfrac{(T-4)!+(T-5)!+(T-6)!}{3!}}$. (The notation $n!$ means the product of all the positive integers from $1$ to $n$.)

solutions.title: Factor out
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from C3.) $6!+5!+4!=4!\,(30+5+1)=24\cdot36=864$, and $864/3!=864/6=144$, whose square root is $12$.

**Answer: $12$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question D2

prompt: Let $T=6$. The straight line $2x+3y=2T$ cuts the $y$-axis at $A$. The straight line $3x+2y=2T$ cuts the $x$-axis at $B$. The two lines intersect at $C$. The origin is at $O$. The area of the quadrilateral $OBCA$ is $\dfrac pq$, where $p$ and $q$ are positive integers with no common factor greater than $1$. Find the value of $p-8q$.

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from D1.) The lines are $2x+3y=12$ and $3x+2y=12$. $A=(0,4)$, $B=(4,0)$ and, by symmetry, $C=\left(\frac{12}5,\frac{12}5\right)$. The quadrilateral $OBCA$ splits along $OC$ into triangles $OBC$ and $OCA$, each with base $4$ and height $\frac{12}5$: area $\frac12\cdot4\cdot\frac{12}5=\frac{24}5$. The total is $\frac{48}5$, so $p-8q=48-40=8$.

**Answer: $8$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question D3

prompt: Let $T=8$. The transformation $X$ represents a rotation of $90^\circ$ clockwise about the point $(2,3)$. The transformation $Y$ represents a reflection in the line $y=x$. Andrew applies transformation $X$ to the point $A\left(T-2,\tfrac12T\right)$ and then applies transformation $Y$ to the image to obtain point $B$. Bill applies transformation $Y$ to the point $A$ and then applies transformation $X$ to the image to obtain point $C$. Chris notices that a translation of $\begin{pmatrix}a\\-b\end{pmatrix}$ transforms the point $B$ to the point $C$. Find the value of $ab$.

solutions.title: Follow the points
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from D2.) $A=(6,4)$. A $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation about $(2,3)$ sends a vector $(u,v)$ from the centre to $(v,-u)$. Andrew: $A-(2,3)=(4,1)\mapsto(1,-4)$, so the image is $(3,-1)$; reflecting in $y=x$ gives $B=(-1,3)$. Bill: $Y(A)=(4,6)$, then $(4,6)-(2,3)=(2,3)\mapsto(3,-2)$, so $C=(5,1)$. The translation from $B$ to $C$ is $\begin{pmatrix}6\\-2\end{pmatrix}$, so $a=6$, $b=2$ and $ab=12$.

**Answer: $12$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2018-19 National Final, Shuttle Round, question D4

prompt: Let $T=12$. Find the remainder when $(221^3+221^2+221)\,T$ is divided by $37$.

solutions.title: Work modulo 37
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from D3.) $221=5\cdot37+36\equiv-1\pmod{37}$. So $221^3+221^2+221\equiv-1+1-1=-1$. Then $(221^3+221^2+221)\cdot12\equiv-12\equiv25\pmod{37}$.

**Answer: $25$**
